claim: Electron microscopy of biological tissue has recently seen an unprecedented increase in imaging throughput.
source: Electron microscopy of biological tissue has recently seen an unprecedented increase in imaging throughput moving the ultrastructural analysis of large tissue blocks such as whole brains into the realm of the feasible.
evidence: This is a general statement about recent developments in the field, supported by the citations that follow in the manuscript.

claim: Homogeneous, high-quality electron microscopy staining of large biological samples is still a major challenge.
source: However, homogeneous, high-quality electron microscopy staining of large biological samples is still a major challenge.
evidence: This statement identifies a current limitation in the field, which is supported by the context and subsequent discussion in the manuscript.

claim: Assessing staining quality in electron microscopy requires running a sample through the entire staining protocol end-to-end.
source: To date, assessing the staining quality in electron microscopy requires running a sample through the entire staining protocol end-to-end, which can take weeks or even months for large samples, rendering protocol optimization for such samples to be inefficient.
evidence: This describes the current state of practice in the field before the introduction of the new method.

claim: The staining protocol for large samples can take weeks or even months.
source: To date, assessing the staining quality in electron microscopy requires running a sample through the entire staining protocol end-to-end, which can take weeks or even months for large samples, rendering protocol optimization for such samples to be inefficient.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the time requirements for staining protocols.

claim: The measured accumulation of osmium in fixed tissue obeys empirically a quadratic dependence between the incubation time and sample size.
source: We show that the measured accumulation of osmium in fixed tissue obeys empirically a quadratic dependence between the incubation time and sample size.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Potassium ferrocyanide clears the tissue after osmium staining.
source: We found that potassium ferrocyanide, a classic reducing agent for osmium tetroxide, clears the tissue after osmium staining and that the tissue expands in osmium tetroxide solution, but shrinks in potassium ferrocyanide reduced osmium solution.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Tissue expands in osmium tetroxide solution.
source: We found that potassium ferrocyanide, a classic reducing agent for osmium tetroxide, clears the tissue after osmium staining and that the tissue expands in osmium tetroxide solution, but shrinks in potassium ferrocyanide reduced osmium solution.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Tissue shrinks in potassium ferrocyanide reduced osmium solution.
source: We found that potassium ferrocyanide, a classic reducing agent for osmium tetroxide, clears the tissue after osmium staining and that the tissue expands in osmium tetroxide solution, but shrinks in potassium ferrocyanide reduced osmium solution.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Image acquisition rates of biological electron microscopy facilities have been scaled to 10^7–10^9 pixels per second through parallelization and automation.
source: In the past decade the image acquisition rates of biological electron microscopy facilities have been scaled to 107–109 pixels per second through parallelization and automation (Hayworth et al., 2014; Schalek et al., 2011; Ren and Kruit, 2016; Denk and Horstmann, 2004; Hayworth et al., 2020; Eberle et al., 2015; Graham et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The increase in imaging throughput for biological samples has been mainly driven by the emerging Neuroscience field of connectomics.
source: The increase in imaging throughput for biological samples has been mainly driven by the emerging Neuroscience field of connectomics which aims to densely reconstruct neuronal circuits with synaptic resolution (Briggman et al., 2011; Helmstaedter et al., 2013; Bock et al., 2011; Zheng et al., 2018; Scheffer et al., 2020; Kornfeld et al., 2017; Wanner and Friedrich, 2020; Lee et al., 2016; Kasthuri et al., 2015; Wilson et al., 2019; Schmidt et al., 2017; Svara et al., 2018; Vishwanathan et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to connectomics studies.

claim: Connectomics aims to densely reconstruct neuronal circuits with synaptic resolution.
source: The increase in imaging throughput for biological samples has been mainly driven by the emerging Neuroscience field of connectomics which aims to densely reconstruct neuronal circuits with synaptic resolution (Briggman et al., 2011; Helmstaedter et al., 2013; Bock et al., 2011; Zheng et al., 2018; Scheffer et al., 2020; Kornfeld et al., 2017; Wanner and Friedrich, 2020; Lee et al., 2016; Kasthuri et al., 2015; Wilson et al., 2019; Schmidt et al., 2017; Svara et al., 2018; Vishwanathan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a definition of the field of connectomics, supported by citations.

claim: Analysis of terabyte-sized electron microscopy datasets is becoming increasingly automated using machine-learning and computer vision.
source: Also, the analysis of the terabyte-sized electron microscopy datasets produced by these studies is becoming increasingly automated using machine-learning and computer vision (Januszewski et al., 2018; Dorkenwald et al., 2020; Schubert et al., 2019; Dorkenwald et al., 2017; Berning et al., 2015; Staffler et al., 2017; Jain et al., 2010; Buhmann et al., 2020; Vergara et al., 2020; Turner et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to machine learning and computer vision work.

claim: A remaining obstacle is the lack of reliable tissue processing and staining protocols for large samples where the smallest dimension is greater than 1 mm.
source: However, a remaining obstacle is the lack of reliable tissue processing and staining protocols for large samples where the smallest dimension is greater than 1 mm.
evidence: This identifies a current limitation in the field that the study aims to address.

claim: Existing en bloc electron microscopy staining protocols have been optimized for staining small samples with dimensions of less than 1 mm.
source: Existing en bloc electron microscopy staining protocols have been optimized for staining small samples with dimensions of less than 1 mm (Genoud et al., 2018; Hua et al., 2015; Deerinck et al., 2010; Tapia et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to existing protocols.

claim: Using aldehyde-stabilized cryopreservation the cellular ultrastructure can be preserved even in large tissue blocks with dimensions exceeding 1 mm and entire brains.
source: Using aldehyde-stabilized cryopreservation (McIntyre and Fahy, 2015) the cellular ultrastructure can be preserved even in large tissue blocks with dimensions exceeding 1 mm and entire brains.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work on cryopreservation.

claim: Large en bloc stained samples still suffer from artifacts such as inhomogeneous staining and membrane or tissue cracks.
source: Despite pioneering work on en bloc staining protocols for whole mouse brains (Mikula and Denk, 2015; Mikula et al., 2012), large en bloc stained samples still suffer from artifacts such as inhomogeneous staining and membrane or tissue cracks.
evidence: This identifies current problems with large sample staining, supported by citations.

claim: En bloc sample preparation for electron microscopy generally requires tissue fixation, staining and embedding in resin.
source: En bloc sample preparation for electron microscopy generally requires tissue fixation, staining and embedding in resin.
evidence: This describes the standard procedure in the field.

claim: Macromolecules in tissue are stabilized via crosslinking by diffusing or perfusing buffered solutions of fixatives such as formaldehyde and glutaraldehyde.
source: First, the macromolecules in the tissue are stabilized via crosslinking by diffusing or perfusing buffered solutions of fixatives such as formaldehyde (Claude and Fullam, 1945; Fox et al., 1985) and glutaraldehyde (Sabatini et al., 1964).
evidence: This describes a standard fixation procedure, supported by citations.

claim: Biological tissue is composed mostly of carbon and other low atomic number elements.
source: Because biological tissue is composed mostly of carbon and other low atomic number elements, the tissue is stained with heavy metals to increase the contrast in electron micrographs (Bahr, 1954; Porter et al., 1945).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about biological tissue composition.

claim: Tissue is stained with heavy metals to increase the contrast in electron micrographs.
source: Because biological tissue is composed mostly of carbon and other low atomic number elements, the tissue is stained with heavy metals to increase the contrast in electron micrographs (Bahr, 1954; Porter et al., 1945).
evidence: This describes the purpose of heavy metal staining, supported by citations.

claim: Heavy metal stains are composed of electron dense atoms such as osmium, lead or uranium.
source: These heavy metal stains are composed of electron dense atoms such as osmium, lead or uranium.
evidence: This lists the types of heavy metals used in staining.

claim: Some heavy metals (e.g. osmium) also act as fixatives.
source: In addition, some of these heavy metals (e.g. osmium) also act as fixatives (Bahr, 1955).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: The most commonly used resins are epoxy resins such as araldite or Epon.
source: The most commonly used resins are epoxy resins (Maaløe and Andersen, 1956), such as araldite (Glauert et al., 1956) or Epon (Finck, 1960) because of their thermal stability and electron transparency.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to the original descriptions of these resins.

claim: Epoxy resins are used because of their thermal stability and electron transparency.
source: The most commonly used resins are epoxy resins (Maaløe and Andersen, 1956), such as araldite (Glauert et al., 1956) or Epon (Finck, 1960) because of their thermal stability and electron transparency.
evidence: This explains the rationale for using epoxy resins.

claim: Ultrathin sections (<100 nm) are typically collected from the embedded tissue using an ultramicrotome to inspect staining quality.
source: To inspect the staining quality in an electron microscope, ultrathin sections (<100 nm) are typically collected from the embedded tissue using an ultramicrotome.
evidence: This describes the standard procedure for preparing samples for EM inspection.

claim: Many steps in classic en bloc electron microscopy staining protocols are based on passive diffusion of chemicals into the tissue.
source: Many steps in the classic en bloc electron microscopy staining protocols are based on passive diffusion of chemicals into the tissue.
evidence: This describes a key characteristic of traditional staining protocols.

claim: Passive diffusion is one of the main bottlenecks for preparing large samples (smallest dimension >1 mm) for electron microscopy.
source: Passive diffusion is one of the main bottlenecks for preparing large samples (smallest dimension >1 mm) for electron microscopy (Burkl and Schiechl, 1968; Medawar, 1941).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: For small samples (smallest dimension <1 mm) a typical en bloc staining protocol takes about 10–15 days including sectioning.
source: For small samples (smallest dimension <1 mm) a typical en bloc staining protocol takes about 10–15 days including sectioning (Tapia et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to an established protocol.

claim: For large samples or whole brains, a diffusion-based staining protocol takes several weeks or even months.
source: However, for large samples or whole brains, a diffusion-based staining protocol takes several weeks or even months (Mikula et al., 2012; Mikula and Denk, 2015; Masís et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to protocols for large samples.

claim: Electron microscopy staining is a 'black box' and changes to staining protocols can only be assessed using an electron microscope.
source: To date, electron microscopy staining is a 'black box' and changes to staining protocols can only be assessed using an electron microscope, which in turn requires a sample to be run through the entire staining protocol.
evidence: This describes the current limitation that the study aims to address.

claim: Conventional approaches for optimizing staining protocols rely on sequential screening of hundreds of samples that have been processed end-to-end.
source: Conventional approaches for optimizing the parameters of staining protocols rely on sequential screening of hundreds of samples that have been processed end-to-end.
evidence: This describes the current practice in the field.

claim: Sequential screening is very inefficient for months-long protocols.
source: However, sequential screening is very inefficient for months-long protocols.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the time requirements of the protocols.

claim: X-ray based computed micro-tomography (μCT) has been introduced for a relatively fast, macroscopic assessment of staining quality and tissue integrity of resin-embedded whole mouse brains.
source: Recently, X-ray based computed micro-tomography (μCT) has been introduced for a relatively fast, macroscopic assessment of staining quality and tissue integrity of resin-embedded whole mouse brains (Mikula and Denk, 2015; Kuan et al., 2020; Dyer et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work on μCT.

claim: Mikula and Denk (2015) showed that the pixel intensities of serial-section EM images and the intensity of the corresponding reslice are similar.
source: (Mikula and Denk, 2015) showed that the pixel intensities of serial-section EM images and the intensity of the corresponding reslice are similar.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The osmium diffuses passively from the cortical surface and the brain ventricles into the tissue and forms a staining front of tissue-bound osmium that moves towards the center of the sample as time progresses.
source: The osmium diffuses passively from the cortical surface and the brain ventricles into the tissue and forms a staining front of tissue-bound osmium (large arrowhead) that moves towards the center of the sample as time progresses.
evidence: This is directly observed in the X-ray projection images shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The pixel intensity/X-ray absorption scales linearly with the concentration/density of osmium.
source: The pixel intensity/X-ray absorption scales linearly with the concentration/density of osmium (black line, Pearson correlation coefficient r=0.99, <10–6; n=3 for each concentration).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1c with statistical support.

claim: The propagation of the staining front can be fitted by a quadratic model in which the penetration depth x of the staining front is proportional to the square root of the incubation time t.
source: The propagation can be fitted by a quadratic model (dashed black lines) in which the penetration depth x of the staining front is proportional to the square root of the incubation time t (residual standard error: SEres = 14.68 μm).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1d with model fitting results.

claim: After 20 hr of incubation the staining density of osmium is homogeneous across the first 1000 μm of cortical depth.
source: After 20 hr of incubation the staining density of osmium is homogeneous across the first 1000 μm of cortical depth (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data in Figure 1e.

claim: The ultrastructure is well preserved after 20 hr of incubation in 2% buffered OsO4.
source: In addition, the ultrastructure is well preserved (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the electron microscopy images in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Reduced osmium is known to result in higher contrast for electron microscopy images than non-reduced OsO4.
source: Reduced osmium is another commonly used staining agent that is known to result in higher contrast for electron microscopy images than non-reduced OsO4.
evidence: This is a known fact in the field.

claim: For Ferro-redOs the accumulation of heavy metals peaks at a depth between 300 and 800 μm.
source: Consistent with previous reports on Ferro-redOs staining in large samples (Hua et al., 2015; Mikula and Denk, 2015) we found that for Ferro-redOs the accumulation of heavy metals peaks at a depth between 300 and 800 μm (Figure 1e), whereas the tissue above or below that depth is stained less.
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data in Figure 1e and is consistent with prior reports.

claim: The band of more heavily stained tissue in Ferro-redOs has been traditionally associated with precipitated osmium that hinders the diffusion and prevents homogenous staining.
source: Traditionally, this band of more heavily stained tissue has been associated with precipitated osmium that hinders the diffusion and prevents homogenous staining (Genoud et al., 2018; Hua et al., 2015; Mikula and Denk, 2015), in particular deeper in the tissue.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: No band of heavily stained tissue is present in tissue immersed in non-reduced OsO4.
source: No such band is present in tissue immersed in non-reduced OsO4.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Mikula and Denk (2015) reported that homogeneous staining of large samples with Ferro-redOs was achieved by adding formamide to the Ferro-redOs solution.
source: (Mikula and Denk, 2015) reported that homogeneous staining of large samples with Ferro-redOs was achieved by adding formamide to the Ferro-redOs solution.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The mechanisms by which formamide acts are not known.
source: However, the underlying mechanisms by which formamide acts are not known (Mikula and Denk, 2015; Genoud et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations indicating the lack of understanding.

claim: Mikula and Denk (2015) hypothesized that formamide might prevent precipitation by generally solubilizing compounds or that it might allow highly charged molecules to cross membranes more easily.
source: (Mikula and Denk, 2015) hypothesized that formamide might prevent precipitation by generally solubilizing compounds or that it might allow highly charged molecules to cross membranes more easily.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior work, supported by citation.

claim: Adding formamide to the Ferro-redOs solution resulted in more homogeneous staining.
source: Adding formamide to the Ferro-redOs solution indeed resulted in more homogeneous staining (Figure 1e, )
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data in Figure 1e.

claim: The heavy metal density was lower in Ferro-redOs with formamide than in osmium only.
source: Adding formamide to the Ferro-redOs solution indeed resulted in more homogeneous staining (Figure 1e, ), but the heavy metal density was lower than in osmium only.
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data in Figure 1e.

claim: Mikula and Denk (2015) reported that the tissue tends to expand at high concentrations of formamide (>50%).
source: (Mikula and Denk, 2015) reported that the tissue tends to expand at high concentrations of formamide (>50%).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: For a concentration of 11.25% formamide, the sample height increased by about 15% within 20 hr of incubation.
source: For a concentration of 11.25% formamide, the sample height increased by about 15% within 20 hr of incubation, whereas for a formamide concentration of 5.56%, the tissue height expanded only by approximately 10% (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data in Figure 1f.

claim: For a formamide concentration of 5.56%, the tissue height expanded by approximately 10% within 20 hr of incubation.
source: For a concentration of 11.25% formamide, the sample height increased by about 15% within 20 hr of incubation, whereas for a formamide concentration of 5.56%, the tissue height expanded only by approximately 10% (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data in Figure 1f.

claim: In the first 3 hr of incubation in Ferro-redOs with 5.56% formamide the tissue actually shrank.
source: Note, in the first 3 hr of incubation in Ferro-redOs with 5.56% formamide the tissue actually shrank, suggesting that there are opposite forces acting on the tissue.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: There are opposite forces acting on the tissue during Ferro-redOs incubation with formamide.
source: Note, in the first 3 hr of incubation in Ferro-redOs with 5.56% formamide the tissue actually shrank, suggesting that there are opposite forces acting on the tissue.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of initial shrinkage followed by expansion.

claim: In Ferro-redOs solution without any formamide, the tissue shrank by about 5% in height.
source: Indeed, in Ferro-redOs solution without any formamide, the tissue shrank by about 5% in height (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data in Figure 1f.

claim: In 2% buffered OsO4 solution the sample height expands by about 5%.
source: In contrast, we found that in 2% buffered OsO4 solution the sample height expands by about 5% (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data in Figure 1f.

claim: No sample expansion was found if the reduced osmium solution was prepared with 2.5% potassium ferricyanide K3[Fe(CN)6].
source: However, we found no sample expansion if the reduced osmium solution was prepared with 2.5% potassium ferricyanide K3[Fe(CN)6]+ 8 a,b), another commonly used reducing agent for OsO4.
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Hua et al., 2015 suggested an alternative approach to achieve homogeneous staining in 1 mm brain punches with Ferro-redOs without formamide, in which osmium and the reducing agent are applied separately.
source: Hua et al., 2015 suggested an alternative approach to achieve homogeneous staining in 1 mm brain punches with Ferro-redOs without formamide, in which osmium and the reducing agent are applied separately.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Hua et al., 2015 hypothesized that the main effect of reducing agents such as K4[Fe(CN)6] is to convert VIII-oxidized water-soluble osmium into an VI-oxidized water-soluble form which is thought to generate additional, non-polar OsO2 to be deposited in the membrane.
source: (Hua et al., 2015) hypothesized that the main effect of reducing agents such as K4[Fe(CN)6] is to convert VIII-oxidized water-soluble osmium into an VI-oxidized water-soluble form which is thought to generate additional, non-polar OsO2 to be deposited in the membrane increasing the heavy metal content and the contrast in electron microscopy.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior work, supported by citation.

claim: The heavy metal density in K4[Fe(CN)6] immersed samples did not increase, but rather decreased from the sample surface towards the center as time progressed.
source: However, we found that the heavy metal density in the K4[Fe(CN)6] immersed samples did not increase, but rather decrease from the sample surface towards the center as time progressed (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data in Figure 2a.

claim: K4[Fe(CN)6] removes or 'washes out' osmium from the sample.
source: This suggests that K4[Fe(CN)6] removes or "washes out" osmium from the sample (Litman and Barrnett, 1972) resulting in an inverse staining gradient.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and supported by a citation.

claim: The 'washing effect' of K4[Fe(CN)6] is stronger for longer incubation times as well as close to the sample surface and around blood vessels.
source: This "washing effect" is stronger for longer incubation times as well as close to the sample surface and around blood vessels (anecdotal observation in electron microscopy images, data not shown).
evidence: This is based on observations in the experimental data.

claim: For incubation times longer than 12 hr, K4[Fe(CN)6] readily dissolves and disintegrates the tissue.
source: For incubation times longer than 12 hr, K4[Fe(CN)6] readily dissolves and disintegrates the tissue (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: No 'washing effect' was observed if the same procedure was repeated with 2.5% potassium ferricyanide K3[Fe(CN)6].
source: Interestingly, no 'washing effect' was observed if the same procedure was repeated with 2.5% potassium ferricyanide K3[Fe(CN)6], but the sample height shrank by about 2% (Figure 1—figure supplement 3,f, ).
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Only a small reduction in heavy metal density could be observed when the sample was washed with double-distilled H2O for 20 hr.
source: Similarly, only a small reduction in heavy metal density could be observed when the sample was washed with double-distilled H2O for 20 hr (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: At the beginning of the OsO4 incubation, the density of OsO4 steeply increases and peaks close to the surface of the sample.
source: At the beginning of the OsO4 incubation, the density of OsO4 steeply increases and peaks close to the surface of the sample.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 2b, d, and e.

claim: As the incubation time progresses, the OsO4 continues to diffuse and accumulates deeper in the tissue.
source: As the incubation time progresses, the OsO4 continues to diffuse and accumulates deeper in the tissue (Figure 2b, d and e).
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data in Figure 2b, d, and e.

claim: Due to the curved surface of the cortical tissue sample, the projected tissue thickness is lower and there are fewer binding sites for osmium, which results in a lower density of osmium closer to the sample surface.
source: Due to the curved surface of the cortical tissue sample, the projected tissue thickness is lower (Figure 2f) and there are fewer binding sites for osmium, which results in a lower density of osmium closer to the sample surface (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is explained by the geometry model and shown in the data.

claim: At any given time, the accumulation seems to plateau from the surface towards the center of the sample, indicating that the binding of OsO4 saturates.
source: At any given time, the accumulation seems to plateau from the surface towards the center of the sample, indicating that the binding of OsO4 saturates (Figure 2d and e).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data and interpreted as saturation.

claim: The saturated density in the samples slowly increased over time from about 129 nmol/mm3 after 1 hr of incubation to 160 nmol/mm3 after 10 hr of incubation.
source: However, we found that the saturated density in the samples slowly increased over time from about 129 nmol/mm3 after 1 hr of incubation to 160 nmol/mm3 after 10 hr of incubation (Figure 2b, d and e), while the density of the solution remained stable at about 82 nmol/mm3.
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data in Figure 2b, d, and e.

claim: The density of the osmium solution remained stable at about 82 nmol/mm3.
source: However, we found that the saturated density in the samples slowly increased over time from about 129 nmol/mm3 after 1 hr of incubation to 160 nmol/mm3 after 10 hr of incubation (Figure 2b, d and e), while the density of the solution remained stable at about 82 nmol/mm3.
evidence: This is measured in the experimental data.

claim: Additional binding sites for OsO4 become available slowly over time.
source: This suggests that additional binding sites for OsO4 become available slowly over time.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that saturated density increases over time.

claim: The reactions underlying the 'unmasking' of binding sites are not known.
source: The reactions underlying the 'unmasking' of binding sites are not known, but we hypothesize that it depends at least partially on the availability and the local concentration of unbound, freely diffusing osmium.
evidence: This acknowledges a gap in knowledge and proposes a hypothesis.

claim: The unmasking of binding sites depends at least partially on the availability and the local concentration of unbound, freely diffusing osmium.
source: The reactions underlying the 'unmasking' of binding sites are not known, but we hypothesize that it depends at least partially on the availability and the local concentration of unbound, freely diffusing osmium.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: At the macroscale level, the accumulation of osmium in biological tissue can be described by four coupled processes: passive diffusion, binding to available sites, unmasking of additional binding sites, and tissue expansion.
source: Hence, at the macroscale level, the accumulation of osmium in biological tissue can be described by four coupled processes (Figure 2g): As the osmium diffuses passively into the tissue, it binds to the available binding sites in the tissue and additional binding sites are slowly being unmasked, while the tissue expands by around 5% within 20 hr of incubation (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is the proposed model based on the experimental observations.

claim: The binding of osmium appears to be nearly instantaneous.
source: While the binding of osmium appears to be nearly instantaneous, the passive diffusion and unmasking reactions are slow and appear to be rate-limiting for the staining.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetics observed in the experimental data.

claim: The passive diffusion and unmasking reactions are slow and appear to be rate-limiting for the staining.
source: While the binding of osmium appears to be nearly instantaneous, the passive diffusion and unmasking reactions are slow and appear to be rate-limiting for the staining.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetics observed in the experimental data.

claim: The fitted parameters of the diffusion-reaction-advection model capture the measured diffusion-reaction-advection kinetics of osmium staining well.
source: The fitted parameters of the diffusion-reaction-advection model (Figure 2—figure supplement 4) capture the measured diffusion-reaction-advection kinetics of osmium staining well (Figure 2c; residual standard error SEres = 0.026 ± 0.005, mean ±s.d.).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the model fitting results shown in Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: In situ X-ray-assisted staining is a new tool for monitoring the different steps of en bloc staining protocols for electron microscopy.
source: In situ X-ray-assisted staining is a new tool for monitoring the different steps of en bloc staining protocols for electron microscopy.
evidence: This is the main contribution of the study.

claim: X-ray-assisted staining enables, for the first time, to observe directly the diffusion of heavy metals and their microscopic effects on the tissue.
source: By opening the 'black box' of staining protocols, X-ray-assisted staining enables, for the first time, to observe directly the diffusion of heavy metals and their microscopic effects on the tissue.
evidence: This describes the novelty and capability of the new method.

claim: X-ray-assisted staining will particularly accelerate and facilitate the development and optimization of new staining protocols for large biological samples such as whole brains.
source: While the technique will be useful to develop novel staining protocols for small to intermediate sized samples with dimensions less than 1 mm, it will particularly accelerate and facilitate the development and optimization of new staining protocols for large biological samples such as whole brains (Figure 1g).
evidence: This is a claim about the potential impact of the method.

claim: The tissue height increased by 5% in buffered osmium solution.
source: In particular, we found that the tissue height increased by 5% in buffered osmium solution, while the tissue height decreased by 5% in buffered Ferro-redOs solution.
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data in Figure 1f.

claim: The tissue height decreased by 5% in buffered Ferro-redOs solution.
source: In particular, we found that the tissue height increased by 5% in buffered osmium solution, while the tissue height decreased by 5% in buffered Ferro-redOs solution.
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data in Figure 1f.

claim: The shrinkage in Ferro-redOs could provide a mechanistic explanation for the long standing issue of diffusion barrier formation in large samples during Ferro-redOs incubation.
source: We hypothesize that this shrinkage could provide a mechanistic explanation for the long standing issue of diffusion barrier formation in large samples during Ferro-redOs incubation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their observations.

claim: K4[Fe(CN)6] could clear the cytosol more efficiently than the cell membranes.
source: A potential explanation could be that K4[Fe(CN)6] clears the cytosol more efficiently than the cell membranes.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation proposed by the authors.

claim: The osmium content in the cytosol gets washed out more/faster by K4[Fe(CN)6], which might result in an overall electron microscopic contrast increase between the membranes and the cytosol.
source: As a consequence, the osmium content in the cytosol gets washed out more/faster, which might result in an overall electron microscopic contrast increase between the membranes and the cytosol.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation proposed by the authors.

claim: The chemical mechanisms by which K4[Fe(CN)6] interact with the tissue remain poorly understood.
source: However, the chemical mechanisms by which K4[Fe(CN)6] interact with the tissue remain poorly understood and shining a light on those processes will require additional work.
evidence: This acknowledges a gap in knowledge.

claim: X-ray assisted staining opens the door for in silico staining protocol optimization.
source: X-ray assisted staining opens the door for in silico staining protocol optimization, by enabling to measure important heavy metal staining parameters such as the effective diffusion coefficients and reaction rate constants directly in situ.
evidence: This describes the potential application of the method.

claim: Osmium diffuses passively into the tissue and binds there quickly to available binding sites, for example unsaturated lipids.
source: Osmium diffuses passively into the tissue and binds there quickly to available binding sites, for example unsaturated lipids.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on experimental observations.

claim: The tissue expands by about 5% in height during osmium staining.
source: Thereby the tissue expands by about 5% in height.
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data in Figure 1f.

claim: Additional binding sites are being unmasked over the course of hours, which enables the tissue to accumulate additional osmium.
